newsitem.title: DUBAI: India's opening up seen boosting Dubai gold trade.
newsitem.headline: India's opening up seen boosting Dubai gold trade.

text.p: Any further liberalisation of the gold market in the Indian subcontinent was unlikely to threaten Dubai's position as a major trading entrepot to the world's biggest market for the yellow metal, analysts said on Saturday.

Delegates at a conference said the emirate's decades-old reputation as a gold redistribution centre, its developed infrastructure, low crime level and relatively high-rated banks were likely to continue to give Dubai the edge despite some analysts' questioning of its future once India is fully open.

"My feeling is if India liberalises completely this place is going to have a bigger share than it has now," prominent Dubai gold trader Harish Pawani said, adding: "Security is a big thing. You see people pushing wheelbarrows freely around the souk, sometimes carrying half a tonne at a time."

Dubai is a major feeder market of gold into India -- the world's single largest consumer of the precious metal -- and Pakistan. Last year Dubai imported 350 tonnes. India consumed some 500 tonnes, about 100 tonnes of which were recycled scrap.

India and Pakistan have in recent years opened up their gold markets. In 1990 India lifted a ban on gold imports, gradually allowing expatriate Indians to bring five kg (11 lb) home once every six months. Early this year the allowance was doubled.
"The supply of gold into Dubai will increase, rather than fall, with the liberalisation of India and Pakistan," said Arif Lakhani, chief executive of Habib Bank AG Zurich in Dubai.
"Dubai shipped about 35 tonnes to Pakistan in the past year. Our estimate this year is about 60 tonnes. Banks in Dubai are in a position to do more shipments to the subcontinent," he added.
Sunil Kashyap of Standard Chartered Bank stressed the importance of banks with good credit ratings in facilitating gold trade between India and Dubai.
Others peppered the upbeat analyses with caution. "If it is cheaper to get the gold directly from source, traders in India might bypass Dubai if India is opened up further," one said.
Some delegates foresaw changes in the supply flow to Dubai.

Jeffrey Rhodes, general manager of the Dubai representative office of Standard Bank London, part of Standard Bank Investment Corp, said: "In the coming years gold will come directly from Johannesburg to Dubai at the expense of Zurich. What is important is to have more direct flights."
World Gold Council data show most Dubai imports in 1996 came from Switzerland, followed by Britain and then South Africa.

Phil Mostert of South Africa's Rand Refinery said: "The previous political dispensation in South Africa did not allow us to market gold directly. The new Mandela government allows us to do this, and I can only see it increasing."
Mohammed Shakachi, director of the Emirates Gold refinery said the issue was a "matter of premiums" -- referring to any price difference between Europe and South African sourced gold.
But trader Pawani said: "Only if the premium exceeds say 25 cents per ounce then we will see a change in the supply routes."
